findings.claim: Coarse-grained rocks have crystals large enough to see with the naked eye (generally above 1 mm). Fine-grained rocks have crystals too small to see individually without a hand lens.
findings.truth: The specification gives the igneous grain-size boundaries as coarse >3 mm and fine <1 mm. Putting the coarse boundary at 1 mm deletes the medium band and contradicts the value the student is given for hand-specimen identification.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2 skills column: 'crystal size [coarse >3 mm, fine <1mm]'

findings.claim: dolerite (medium-grained intermediate intrusive)
findings.truth: Dolerite is a basic (mafic) rock, 45-52% silica, chemically the same as basalt and gabbro. It is intermediate in GRAIN SIZE between basalt and gabbro, not in composition.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Diabase' (dolerite): mafic, 45-52% SiO2, medium-grained equivalent of gabbro/basalt

findings.claim: Examiner reports consistently note that students lose marks by using rock names not on the specification.
findings.truth: No examiner report is cited or verifiable. The claim invents a source. The underlying advice is sound and is kept without the invented attribution.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Under plane-polarised light, different minerals show different colours and extinction angles.
findings.truth: Extinction angles are seen only under crossed polars, not under plane-polarised light. Under plane-polarised light you see colour, shape, relief and cleavage.
findings.evidence: standard optical mineralogy; extinction is a crossed-polar phenomenon

findings.claim: look for crystal shape (angular crystals = fast cooling; well-formed euhedral crystals = slow cooling)
findings.truth: Crystal shape records the order of growth and the space available, not the cooling rate. Rapidly cooled basalt contains euhedral plagioclase laths; slowly cooled granite contains anhedral quartz that crystallised last and filled the gaps. The rule as written is backwards.
findings.evidence: standard igneous petrography (euhedral = grew early into free space; anhedral = grew last)

findings.claim: Writing “hornfels” or “anorthite” when identifying a hand specimen will score nothing — use only the names listed on your data sheet.
findings.truth: Hornfels is a rock, not a mineral, so it is a category error in a list of mineral-naming mistakes. The absolute 'will score nothing' is also an invented mark-scheme claim.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1 lists minerals only; hornfels is a contact-metamorphic rock (named as such in lesson 7)

findings.claim: examiners will not credit it without supporting properties
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about examiner behaviour. The advice itself is right; the promise about marking is not verifiable.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Clay minerals in a mudstone transform into mica, chlorite and then garnet as temperature and pressure increase
findings.truth: The Barrovian index-mineral sequence with increasing grade is chlorite, then biotite (mica), then garnet. Mica and chlorite are the wrong way round.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Metamorphic zone': prograde sequence chlorite - biotite - garnet - staurolite - kyanite - sillimanite

findings.claim: lower-temperature fluids at depth produce more soluble minerals including carbonates
findings.truth: Hydrothermal zoning is controlled by distance from the heat source. The coolest fluids are the ones furthest from the intrusion, not the deepest. Temperature rises with depth, so 'lower-temperature at depth' reverses the relationship the paragraph is describing.
findings.evidence: standard hydrothermal zoning (e.g. Cornish tin-copper-lead-zinc-carbonate zones outward from the granite)

findings.claim: In extended-response questions, three distinct formation mechanisms with a clear mechanism for each will reach the top band.
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme threshold. The spec asks for a sustained, coherent line of reasoning, not a count of mechanisms.
findings.evidence: spec, extended response statement: 'sufficient length to allow them to demonstrate their ability to construct and develop a sustained line of reasoning'

findings.claim: mixing the two terms is a documented examiner concern
findings.truth: No document is cited. The claim invents a source.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag the confusion between porosity and permeability as one of the highest-frequency errors in this unit.
findings.truth: Invents both a source and a frequency statistic. The advice that follows it is correct and is kept.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: 'turbidite current' used five times, and the glossary defines 'turbidite' as 'A submarine density current carrying a mixture of sediment and water...'
findings.truth: A turbidity CURRENT is the flow. A turbidite is the DEPOSIT it leaves - a graded bed, which the spec lists as a deep-marine rock type. The lesson defines the rock as if it were the current. The lesson's own 6-mark mark scheme uses 'turbidity current' correctly, which confirms the error.
findings.evidence: spec 1.3e Deep marine: [turbidites, black shale] - turbidites are rocks; standard sedimentology

findings.claim: The sequence coal — seat earth (fossil soil) — shale — limestone, repeating, is the classic Carboniferous cyclothem.
findings.truth: Read upwards, the cyclothem runs limestone, shale, sandstone, seat earth, coal. The seat earth is the soil the coal-forming plants grew in, so it always lies BELOW the coal. The lesson lists the sequence in reverse and drops the sandstone.
findings.evidence: standard Yoredale / Coal Measures cyclothem; seat earth is by definition the palaeosol under a coal seam

findings.claim: A large, irregular deep intrusion of granite that forms the bulk of the crust is called a _____.
findings.truth: A pluton does not form the bulk of the crust. The keyed answer (pluton) is right, but the stem teaches a false fact. The lesson's own text says a pluton is recognised because erosion strips the cover and exposes it.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2e [lava flows, sills, dykes and plutons]; lesson 4 own text

findings.claim: Plutons are always younger than the rocks they intrude and older than any dykes or sills they feed.
findings.truth: The first half is the correct cross-cutting rule. The second half is not safe: a dyke fed by a pluton froze while the pluton was still molten, so the dyke rock can be the older solid. Cutting the clause leaves the rule the spec needs.
findings.evidence: cross-cutting relationships; the fed dyke and its parent pluton are one intrusive episode

findings.claim: Repeated across lessons 1, 3 and 7: 'Only spec-listed minerals earn marks', 'None of these earn any credit', 'do not use gneiss or hornfels in your answers', and the shortcut 'If your hand specimen is coarse-grained and dark, it is peridotite.'
findings.truth: Two options. (a) Keep: the spec names exactly four igneous rocks (peridotite, basalt, andesite, granite) and four metamorphic rocks (slate, schist, marble, metaquartzite), so hand-specimen answers come from those lists and the guidance is sound teaching. (b) Soften: the rule is stated as a mark-scheme certainty that no published document supports, and 'coarse + dark = peridotite' is false outside the spec's four-rock frame (a coarse dark rock is usually gabbro). Recommendation: (a) keep the scope guidance, because the spec list is genuinely closed; the invented examiner attribution behind it is fixed separately in F3.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2b and 1.4b named rock lists
findings.ruling: Leave: closed spec lists make the rule defensible once the invented source is gone.

findings.claim: if you write that a rock “partially melted” during metamorphism you will lose marks
findings.truth: A mark claim rather than a fact claim, but the underlying rule (metamorphism is solid-state; melting makes it igneous) is correct at GCSE. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: spec 1.4a: recrystallisation to form new minerals

findings.claim: Lesson descriptions run over the 100-character house limit: lesson 4 = 105, lesson 6 = 113, lesson 7 = 102 characters.
findings.truth: Length only, no factual error. Flagged so a later trim pass can pick them up.
findings.evidence: house validator limit

findings.claim: Metallic lustre always indicates either a native metal or a metallic ore mineral.
findings.truth: 'Always' overreaches, but it holds for every mineral on the data sheet (galena, haematite), so it will not mislead a student in this course.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1a named minerals

findings.claim: Slope angle comparison questions require you to state a measurement or comparative value, not just “one is steeper”.
findings.truth: An invented requirement, but harmless advice for a practical-skills question. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix B, jelly lava flow simulation

summary: Sixteen fixes across all seven lessons: one HIGH (lesson 3 gives the coarse igneous grain-size boundary as 1 mm where the spec sets 3 mm) and fifteen MEDIUM. The unit has two systematic faults - five invented examiner-report or mark-scheme claims, and a repeated confusion of 'turbidite' (the rock) with 'turbidity current' (the flow). No lesson names the exam board, and no lesson makes a wrong exam-structure, tier or SPaG claim; every knowledge-check answer key and match order is correct.
